summary: This document describes how OSPFv3 can configure itself automatically, as needed in environments like IPv6 home networks, where users expect to plug in a router and have it use OSPFv3 for routing within the network without manual setup.

eli5.summary: You plug a new router into your home network and it just works out how to talk to the others with no fuss. This explains how.

questions: how does ospfv3 pick a router id
what is the ospfv3 router hardware fingerprint
how are duplicate ospfv3 router ids resolved
subtitle: How OSPFv3 routers can configure themselves, pick unique Router IDs and sort out clashes with no human setup.

tldr.problem: OSPFv3 normally needs manual configuration, such as a unique Router ID, which does not suit places like IPv6 home networks where users just plug in a router.
tldr.mechanism: Autoconfigured routers use defaults (area 0, all IPv6 interfaces), tolerate different hello and dead intervals, pick a pseudorandom Router ID, and detect duplicate Router IDs with a new Autoconfiguration LSA carrying a hardware fingerprint.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 5340 by relaxing the HelloInterval/RouterDeadInterval check and adding hysteresis to self-originated LSA processing. Security and complete autoconfiguration pull in opposite directions.

today: RFC 7503 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2015. It updates RFC 5340 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why OSPFv3 Needs Autoconfiguration
sections.content:
OSPFv3 is a candidate for environments where autoconfiguration is a requirement, such as the IPv6 home network where a user expects to plug in a router and have it use OSPFv3 for routing inside the network. This document describes extensions that make that possible while leaving the protocol largely unchanged from the base specification, RFC 5340.

It covers default configuration, interval flexibility, minimal authentication, unique Router ID generation, adjacency formation, duplicate Router ID resolution and self-originated LSA processing. It updates RFC 5340 in two backward-compatible ways: adjacencies may form between routers with differing HelloIntervals or RouterDeadIntervals, and processing of stale self-originated LSAs gets hysteresis.
sections.eli5: The goal is a router that works the moment you plug it in, like a lamp. The rules stay almost the same as normal OSPFv3.

sections.title: Defaults and Flexible Timers
sections.content:
An autoconfigured router chooses defaults. All autoconfigured interfaces MUST be in area 0. OSPFv3 SHOULD run on all IPv6-capable interfaces, though an interface may be skipped when it is clearly not needed, for example one facing an ISP. Interface types follow Layer 2: Ethernet and Wi-Fi become broadcast networks and PPP becomes point-to-point. Interfaces SHOULD use Interface Instance ID 0 for the base IPv6 unicast instance, and 64 for a separate IPv4 unicast instance.

Autoconfigured routers also do not need identical timers. The received HelloInterval is ignored, and the received RouterDeadInterval sets the Neighbor Inactivity Timer for that neighbor, so neighbors on a link may use different values. A router not supporting autoconfiguration still requires identical values to form an adjacency.

On back-to-back Ethernet links the router would otherwise wait RouterDeadInterval seconds before forming an adjacency. An autoconfigured router MAY shorten that wait to a value no less than HelloInterval + 1, at the cost of slightly more risk of the Designated Router flapping.
sections.eli5: The router picks sensible settings on its own, and it does not mind if its neighbors check in at different speeds.

sections.title: Minimal Authentication
sections.content:
In many deployments, the need for authentication overrides the goal of full autoconfiguration. So routers supporting this specification are RECOMMENDED to offer at least an option to configure a single password for HMAC-SHA authentication as in the OSPFv3 Authentication Trailer (RFC 7166).

The password is RECOMMENDED to be entered as ASCII hexadecimal digits, with 32 or more digits accepted so it can have high entropy. It is used on all autoconfigured interfaces, with the Security Association Identifier set to 1 and HMAC-SHA-256 as the algorithm.
sections.eli5: If you want a lock, you set one shared password and every link uses it. You do not have to set up anything per link.

sections.title: Router ID Selection and Adjacency Formation
sections.content:
Every OSPFv3 router needs a Router ID unique in its routing domain. The usual selection methods depend on a unique IPv4 interface address, which an autoconfigured deployment is unlikely to have. So a pseudorandom number SHOULD be used, seeded with something likely to be unique, such as part or a hash of the Router-Hardware-Fingerprint. Routers SHOULD keep the last successfully chosen Router ID in nonvolatile storage, to avoid collisions after the router is first added.

OSPFv3 protocol messages use IPv6 link-local addresses, so adjacency formation can proceed as soon as a Router ID is chosen and the link-local address has finished Duplicate Address Detection under RFC 4862. Apart from the timer flexibility above and duplicate Router ID handling, nothing else changes.
sections.eli5: The router rolls a big random number as its name and writes it down so it keeps the same name next time.

sections.title: Duplicate Router ID Detection and Resolution
sections.content:
Random IDs can collide, so there are two detection cases. For a directly connected neighbor, a clash is seen when a valid OSPFv3 packet arrives with the same Router ID but a different IPv6 link-local source address. The router with the numerically smaller link-local address must pick a new Router ID.

For non-neighbors, every autoconfiguring router MUST originate an Autoconfiguration (AC) LSA carrying a Router-Hardware-Fingerprint TLV, a variable-length value that very probably identifies the router uniquely. A router that receives an AC LSA bearing its own Router ID compares the fingerprint with its own. If they differ, the router with the numerically smaller fingerprint MUST choose a new Router ID.

The loser SHOULD first check its link state database for an AC LSA with the new ID and a different fingerprint. After switching, it MUST reoriginate all its self-originated LSAs and re-establish its adjacencies. The router that keeps the ID reoriginates or flushes stale self-originated LSAs as RFC 2328 describes.
sections.eli5: Each router carries a unique serial-number-like fingerprint. If two have the same name, the one with the smaller fingerprint picks a new name.

sections.title: The Autoconfiguration LSA
sections.content:
The AC LSA has function code 15, with the S2/S1 bits set to 01 for Area Flooding Scope and the U bit set so it is flooded even if not understood. Its Link State ID is an index to tell apart multiple AC LSAs from one router; only LSID 0 is described. The body is a list of TLVs in the format used by RFC 3630: a type, a length of the value in octets, and the value padded to 4-octet alignment. Unrecognized types are ignored.

The first TLV defined is the Router-Hardware-Fingerprint, type 1. It MUST be in the AC LSA with LSID 0, SHOULD occur at most once, and the first instance takes precedence. Its length is variable but must be 32 octets or greater. If it is not the first TLV, the LSA is considered malformed, ignored for duplicate detection, and the event SHOULD be logged.

The fingerprint MUST have an extremely high probability of uniqueness and be based on hardware attributes that do not change across hard and soft restarts. It SHOULD be built from several local values such as MAC addresses, CPU ID or serial numbers, and including a universal token such as an IEEE 802 48-bit MAC address or an EUI-64 identifier is RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The fingerprint is a long ID built from things like the router's hardware addresses and serial numbers, so no two routers share one.

sections.title: Security and Self-Originated LSA Hysteresis
sections.content:
The goals of security and complete autoconfiguration are somewhat contradictory. With no explicit security configuration, any device added to the network is adopted automatically. Autoconfiguration can be combined with the password above, or with OSPFv3 IPsec or other Authentication Trailer algorithms at the cost of more configuration.

A router with a duplicate Router ID, accidental or malicious, is an attack point: its LSAs look self-originated to the real owner, which tries to flush them. To mitigate this, the RFC changes Section 13.4 of RFC 2328. When a router sees the same self-originated LSAs repeatedly flushed or reoriginated, it SHOULD delay processing for recently handled LSAs. The RFC recommends 10 seconds as the interval defining recent processing and an exponential back-off of 1 to 8 seconds for the delay. This MAY also be used outside autoconfigured deployments, and the condition SHOULD be logged.
sections.eli5: If a pretender uses your name, the two of you could keep undoing each other's work. So the router waits a bit longer each time to give the clash time to be sorted out.

sections.title: Management and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
Routers supporting this specification are RECOMMENDED to also support explicit OSPFv3 configuration, so autoconfigured values can be overridden, for instance when multiple areas are needed, and to allow autoconfiguration to be disabled completely. Manual Router IDs are RECOMMENDED where a Router ID change would disrupt routing too much. Routers MUST indicate in their operational state display whether they and their interfaces were autoconfigured.

IANA allocated value 15 in the OSPFv3 LSA Function Codes registry for the AC LSA, and created a registry for AC LSA TLVs, allocated by IETF Review or, in exceptional circumstances, IESG Approval. The initial values are 0 (Reserved), 1 (Router-Hardware-Fingerprint) and 65535 (Autoconfiguration-Experiment-TLV).
sections.eli5: People can still set things by hand, and the router tells you which settings it made up itself.
